title: Exploring Chemical Information in PubChem
author: Kim
materials: Web browser (Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Safari, or Firefox)
spreadsheet software (Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets)
An up‐to‐date Web browser, such as Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Safari, or Firefox, is required for this protocol (and all other protocols in this article)

An up‐to‐date Web browser, such as Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Safari, or Firefox, is required for this protocol (and all other protocols in this article)In addition, this protocol requires a text file containing the CIDs of the hit compounds returned from Basic Protocol 2. This file can be generated from the CSV file downloaded in Basic Protocol 2. Open the CSV file in spreadsheet software (e.g., Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets). Copy the first column containing the CIDs (except for the column header), paste them into a text editor (e.g., Notepad on Windows PC and TextEdit on Mac), and save them as a text file. In this protocol, the file name is assumed to be mycids.txt. Double‐check that the file has the same format as the mycids.txt file in Figure 5 (e.g., one CID for each line).

Basic Protocol 6 is designed to demonstrate how to download the bioactivity data of all chemicals tested against a given protein and how to quickly access data for a protein orthologous to another protein, using the human type‐1 angiotensin II receptor and its rat ortholog as an example. This protocol is similar to Basic Protocol 5, which downloads the list of drugs interacting with the gene encoding type‐1 angiotensin II receptor. However, it should be kept in mind that a gene record in PubChem can be associated with multiple protein records, reflecting the fact that a gene can produce multiple protein sequences (e.g., isoforms or variants). Because bioassays archived in PubChem were performed typically against one of the multiple protein sequences that may arise from a single gene, the Summary pages of the different proteins from the same gene present different sets of bioactivity data. These data are merged together and presented on the Summary page of the encoding gene. Therefore, extra care should be taken when downloading the bioactivity data from the Summary page of a gene or protein.

steps.title: Search losartan and retrieve interactors
steps.instruction: Open an up‑to‑date web browser, go to PubChem, enter “losartan” in the text search box, select the best hit (CID 3961), and on its Summary page locate the sections listing interacting genes and proteins from sources such as DrugBank, CTD, DGIdb, IUPHAR/BPS, ChEMBL and PDB.

steps.title: 2‑D similarity search with Lipinski filters
steps.instruction: From the losartan Summary page, click the CID 3961 link to start a 2‑D similarity search, choose “2‑D similarity”, and apply filters for Lipinski’s rule of five (molecular weight, hydrogen‑bond donor/acceptor counts, rotatable bond count, etc.). Optionally adjust the “Search All” setting if more than 1 000 hits are expected. Download the filtered hit list (including computed properties) as a CSV file to the local computer.

steps.title: 3‑D similarity search and download structures
steps.instruction: Using the same CID 3961, launch a 3‑D similarity search, accept the default settings, and after results appear, download the 3‑D structures of the returned compounds in SDF format to the local computer.

steps.title: Download 3‑D similarity scores via Score Matrix Service
steps.instruction: Visit https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/score_matrix, upload the list of CIDs obtained from the 2‑D similarity search (or paste them), select “3‑D similarity” as the score type, and request the matrix. Save the returned CID‑CID‑score triples (or matrix) to a file.

steps.title: Create mycids.txt from the CSV file
steps.instruction: Open the CSV file saved in step 2 with spreadsheet software (e.g., Excel or Google Sheets), copy the first column containing the CIDs (exclude the header), paste the values into a plain‑text editor, place one CID per line, and save the file as mycids.txt. Verify that the file matches the format shown in Figure 5 (one CID per line).

steps.title: Substructure search and download bioactivity data
steps.instruction: In PubChem, open the Sketcher, draw or paste the substructure corresponding to CID 15207942, run a substructure search, and on the results page click the “Linked Data Sets” button to retrieve associated BioAssay data. Download the bioactivity data to the local computer.

steps.title: Find drugs targeting the human angiotensin‑II receptor gene
steps.instruction: Search PubChem for the gene name of the human type‑1 angiotensin‑II receptor, filter the gene list by taxonomy to retain only human entries, open the gene’s Summary page, and download the listed drug compounds (sourced from DrugBank, ChEMBL, IUPHAR/BPS).

steps.title: Download bioactivity data for receptor and ortholog
steps.instruction: From the protein Summary pages of the human type‑1 angiotensin‑II receptor and its rat ortholog, use the “Download” option to obtain all BioAssay records for chemicals tested against each protein. Merge or compare the datasets as needed, noting that gene‑level Summary pages aggregate data from multiple protein isoforms.

steps.title: Retrieve chemicals sharing MeSH therapeutic annotations
steps.instruction: Open the PubChem Classification Browser, perform a search for the MeSH term “Antihypertensive Agents”, repeat for “Anti‑Arrhythmia Agents”, and use the Boolean AND operator (or intersect the two result sets) to obtain chemicals annotated with both terms. Export the intersected list.

steps.title: Identity search for valsartan stereoisomers and isotopomers
steps.instruction: Search PubChem for valsartan (CID 60846). Run an identity search three times: (a) default settings (connectivity + stereochemistry + isotopism); (b) ignore stereochemistry to retrieve stereoisomers; (c) ignore isotopism to retrieve isotopomers. Download the resulting CID lists for each case.
